title: Project Deadline Manager
learning_objectives: Manage a multi-week project with dependencies

events.description: You're launching the school newspaper in 6 weeks. Tasks and dependencies: Content planning (Week 1) → Article writing (Weeks 2-3) → Editing (Week 4) → Layout design (Week 5) → Printing (Week 6). Meanwhile, ad sales (Weeks 1-3) and photography (Weeks 2-4) run in parallel. What's your critical path?

choices.label: Content → Writing → Editing → Layout → Print (the longest chain)
choices.effect: Correct! This chain has zero slack time. Any delay here delays the whole project.

choices.label: Everything is critical — no room for error
choices.effect: Good caution, but parallel tasks (ads, photos) have some flexibility. The key chain is content through printing.

choices.label: Start all possible tasks immediately
choices.effect: Proactive! Starting parallel tasks early builds buffer time. Smart resource management.

events.description: Week 2: Two of your best writers have a school trip and will miss 3 days. That's 30% of the writing phase. How do you adjust?

choices.label: Redistribute their articles to other writers
choices.effect: Other writers take on 1-2 extra articles each. The writing deadline holds!

choices.label: Extend writing into Week 4, compress editing
choices.effect: Writing gets 3 more days, editing is compressed. Tighter for editors but the critical path holds.

choices.label: Reduce from 20 articles to 16 — quality over quantity
choices.effect: Fewer articles but better ones! Scope reduction is a legitimate project management tool.

events.description: Week 4: The editing team finds that 5 articles need major rewrites. The layout designer says they need final articles by end of Week 5 or printing gets pushed. What's the plan?

choices.label: Start layout with finished articles, edit the 5 in parallel
choices.effect: 11 articles go to layout now, 5 more slot in as they're finished. Parallel work saves the deadline!

choices.label: Weekend editing sprint — all hands on the 5 articles
choices.effect: The team rallies! All 16 articles ready by Monday. Extra effort saves the timeline.

choices.label: Push printing back 3 days, communicate the delay
choices.effect: Transparent communication! You inform the principal and adjust. Better a 3-day delay than a rushed product.

events.description: Week 5: The principal asks if you can add a 4-page special section on the upcoming science fair. That's scope creep — more pages means more layout time and higher printing costs. How do you handle it?

choices.label: Offer 2 pages now, full section in issue #2
choices.effect: Compromise! The principal gets coverage, you keep the timeline. Promise more in the next issue.

choices.label: Accept it but request 1 extra week for launch
choices.effect: Honest about the timeline impact! Adding scope means adding time. The principal agrees.

choices.label: Ask the team if they can handle it in the current timeline
choices.effect: The team votes: 2 pages they can handle, 4 is too much. You counter-propose 2 pages to the principal.

events.description: Launch day! The newspaper is printed and ready for distribution. What did you learn about project management?

choices.label: Critical path management keeps projects on track
choices.effect: The critical path concept saved you from panic when delays hit non-critical tasks.

choices.label: Communicating early about problems prevents bigger problems
choices.effect: Transparency with stakeholders built trust and gave you room to adjust.

choices.label: Plans change — the skill is adjusting while keeping the goal
choices.effect: No project goes exactly to plan. Your ability to adapt is the real skill!

recap_template: You managed a complex project from planning to launch! You identified critical paths, handled delays, managed scope changes, and communicated with stakeholders. These are professional-level project management skills.
positive_framing_rules: Never say the project is falling apart or at risk
Frame delays as normal project challenges with solutions
ai_variation_allowed: Vary the specific delays and challenges

title: College App Timeline

events.description: It's September. You're applying to 6 schools: 2 early action (Nov 1 deadline), 4 regular decision (Jan 1). Each needs: essays, recommendations (ask 6 weeks ahead), test scores (sent 4 weeks ahead), activities list, and financial aid forms. How do you start?

choices.label: Work backward from Nov 1 — what needs to start NOW?
choices.effect: Backward planning! Recommendations need asking by Sept 20, test scores sent by Oct 1, essays drafted by Oct 15. Clear timeline!

choices.label: Start with tasks shared across all apps (activities list, common essay)
choices.effect: Efficient! The common app essay and activities list work for all 6 schools. Do them once, use them everywhere.

choices.label: Focus on your top-choice school's early action first
choices.effect: Top choice gets your best energy! Once that's submitted, you can adapt materials for other schools.

events.description: October: You have 3 essays to write, SAT scores to send, and a teacher says they need 3 more weeks for your recommendation (pushing past Nov 1). Meanwhile, midterms are next week.

choices.label: Ask a different teacher who can meet the deadline
choices.effect: New recommender, same quality! Sometimes backup plans are the best plans.

choices.label: Move that school from early action to regular decision
choices.effect: Strategic pivot! Regular decision gives the original teacher time. One less Nov 1 deadline reduces stress too.

choices.label: Send a polite reminder with the deadline
choices.effect: The teacher apologizes and prioritizes yours! Sometimes a gentle nudge is all that's needed. Advocacy skills!

events.description: November: Early action apps submitted! But now you have 4 regular decision apps, 3 scholarship deadlines (Dec 15, Jan 15, Feb 1), and the FAFSA (financial aid) due by Jan 1. Plus finals in December. How do you map the next 2 months?

choices.label: Block every deadline on a calendar, work backward from each
choices.effect: Visual timeline! You can see exactly when crunch periods overlap and plan rest days around them.

choices.label: Batch similar tasks: all essays one week, all forms another
choices.effect: Batching reduces context-switching! Essay brain one week, form brain the next.

choices.label: Set weekly goals with specific deliverables
choices.effect: Week 1: 2 essays. Week 2: FAFSA + 1 scholarship. Week 3: finals study. Week 4: remaining apps. Clear and achievable!

events.description: December crunch: finals AND application deadlines in the same 2-week window. You're feeling stretched. What's your self-care strategy?

choices.label: Schedule 30-minute breaks between work blocks
choices.effect: Breaks prevent burnout! Research shows regular breaks improve both focus and output quality.

choices.label: Ask family/friends to help with smaller tasks (proofreading, form filling)
choices.effect: Delegating isn't weakness — it's smart management! Your parent proofreads while you focus on essays.

choices.label: Good enough is good enough — stop over-editing
choices.effect: Perfectionism is the enemy of done! Your 4th revision is usually as good as your 10th.

events.description: January 2: Everything is submitted! Looking back at the last 4 months, what's your biggest takeaway about managing long-term timelines?

choices.label: Starting early gave me flexibility when surprises hit
choices.effect: Front-loading work creates buffer time. The recommendation delay didn't become a crisis because you started in September!

choices.label: Having a system (calendar, checklists) kept me sane
choices.effect: Systems beat willpower! When your brain is tired, the system keeps you on track.

choices.label: Taking care of myself made the work better, not slower
choices.effect: Well-rested you produces better essays than burned-out you. Self-care is productivity!

recap_template: You managed 6 college applications across 4 months with overlapping deadlines! You built backward from deadlines, handled surprises, and maintained your well-being. These skills apply to any complex long-term project.
positive_framing_rules: Never say the student is falling behind or stressed out
Frame busy periods as manageable with good planning
Celebrate self-advocacy and self-care as strengths
ai_variation_allowed: Change the number and types of schools

title: Work-Life Balance Sim
learning_objectives: Balance part-time work with academics and social life

events.description: You're a junior with 77 hours/week after school and sleep. Your part-time job wants 15-20 hours, you need ~15 hours for homework/study, and you want time for friends, hobbies, and yourself. How do you allocate your 77 hours?

choices.label: Work 15hr + Study 15hr + Social 10hr + Self-care 7hr = 47hr (30 flex)
choices.effect: Balanced with 30 hours of flex time for meals, commuting, and spontaneous things. Sustainable!

choices.label: Work 20hr + Study 15hr + Social 5hr + Self-care 5hr = 45hr (32 flex)
choices.effect: More money but less social and self-care time. The question is: can you sustain this for months?

choices.label: Work 12hr + Study 20hr + Social 8hr + Self-care 7hr = 47hr (30 flex)
choices.effect: Academic focus! Less income but your GPA will thank you. Depends on your priorities.

events.description: Month 2: Your boss asks you to pick up extra shifts (5 more hours/week). Your grades are good and you could use the money. But your friend says you've been distant lately. What do you do?

choices.label: Decline — your current balance is working
choices.effect: Setting boundaries! 'No' is a complete sentence. Your boss understands and respects it.

choices.label: Take them for 3 weeks only (holiday rush)
choices.effect: Temporary commitment with a clear end date. You earn extra and your friend knows it's short-term.

choices.label: Accept but reduce study time — adjust grades expectation
choices.effect: Conscious trade-off! You accepted lower grades for higher income this month. As long as it's intentional, not accidental.

events.description: Month 4: You notice burnout signs — trouble sleeping, snapping at friends, dreading work. These are signals, not failures. What adjustment do you make?

choices.label: Ask to drop to 12 hours/week at work
choices.effect: Less income but more recovery time. Burnout is expensive — catching it early saves you weeks of suffering.

choices.label: Non-negotiable: 1 hour of self-care daily
choices.effect: Exercise, journaling, or just quiet time. Protecting self-care hours prevents burnout from getting worse.

choices.label: Talk to a counselor, parent, or trusted adult
choices.effect: Asking for help is strength! A counselor helps you see options you couldn't see while stressed.

events.description: End of semester. You've learned a lot about managing your time and energy. What's your biggest insight?

choices.label: Saying no protects what matters most
choices.effect: Boundaries aren't selfish — they're essential. You can't pour from an empty cup.

choices.label: Plans need regular check-ins and adjustments
choices.effect: A monthly review of your time allocation catches problems before they become crises.

choices.label: Priorities change — and that's okay
choices.effect: What mattered in September might shift by February. Regularly reassessing keeps your life aligned with your values.

recap_template: You navigated a semester balancing work, school, social life, and self-care! You learned to set boundaries, recognize burnout, and adjust your plan. Work-life balance is a lifelong skill.
positive_framing_rules: Never say the student is overwhelmed or incapable
Frame burnout signals as useful information, not weakness
ai_variation_allowed: Change the specific work and school scenarios
Vary the burnout signals and responses
